title: Mikey
subtitle: Miguelito, the 1959 Stageway Tour Host
summary: An eight-door 1959 Stageway airport limousine, never bought and never forgotten, reimagined as Miguelito: a Duramax-powered Angeleno tour host who kneels for grandmothers, seats fourteen friends, and runs tacos-to-lobster tours under an open roof.

specifications.platform: 1959 Chevrolet Biscayne 8-door limousine, Armbruster-Stageway Airporter conversion
specifications.engine: GM Duramax L5P 6.6L turbodiesel, compound turbocharged, tuned to purr: a kitten at cruise with the strength kept in reserve
specifications.output: Compound-turbo house spec: about 650 hp and 1,300 lb-ft, turned down for company manners and delivered quietly
specifications.transmission: Allison 1000 6-speed automatic, built for the torque
specifications.rearAxle: GM/AAM 11.5-inch full-float 14-bolt, 3.73, narrowed to the Biscayne
specifications.suspension: Air: lift-biased for breakover on the ~200-inch wheelbase, kneel-for-boarding mode, parade-crawl ride
specifications.steering: Heavy-duty recirculating-ball box, hydraulic assist, chosen for strength
specifications.brakes: Hydroboost, discs as big as the wheels allow
specifications.range: 200+ miles per tank, low-20s gallons, because a good host never watches the gauge
specifications.doors: Eight: forward pairs conventional, rear pairs suicide, center pair opens as a pillar-free French-door gate
specifications.roof: One long open aperture, twin folding canvas halves, grab bars inside (the stiffening ring) and out
specifications.seating: 10 to 14: two front singles with a walk-through, back-to-back bench, central cabinet, rear wraparound
specifications.amenities: The Crystal in the central cabinet, icebox, intercom, narration mic, per-pod reading lights and USB, dual A/C
specifications.wheels: Two sets by suit: hexagonal titanium, 22-in front / 24-in rear, for the tangerine car; painted 16-in steel with dog-dish caps for the green car
specifications.finish: Tangerine candy over copper-bronze, split at the chrome spear, coffee canvas; the formal suit is Brewster greens
specifications.interior: Coffee and cream leather in the tangerine car; deep green leather in the Torpedo manner in the green car
specifications.purpose: Private sightseeing and parade cruising: bespoke Angeleno tours, Mercado tacos to Malibu lobster, sunsets from Mulholland and the Santa Monica Pier
specifications.status: Fantasy: a fully specced design study. The Renton Stageway that inspired it was not purchased.

narrative: Start with the confession, because Miguelito believes a tour should begin with the truth. The blue car in the last photograph is not mine. She is a 1959 Chevrolet Biscayne stretched by Armbruster-Stageway into an eight-door airport limousine, photographed where she sat in Renton, Washington: peeling paint, rust freckles, some glass gone, an Oldsmobile engine keeping her Chevrolet seat warm. I studied her, I priced her, I dreamed over her, and I did not buy her. What came home with me was the idea of her, and the idea has been gaining weight ever since.

The idea has a name and, by now, a face. Miguelito, Mikey to the valets, is a big silver güero of a tour host: a former airporter who spent his working life hauling other people's beginnings and endings, retired into the best job in Los Angeles. He kneels at the curb so your grandmother boards like royalty. He seats fourteen friends without anyone drawing the middle seat. He keeps the Crystal in a cabinet at his center, a microphone by the wheel, and a roof that opens the length of the cabin so the whole party can stand up in the golden hour and watch the city perform. A limousine keeps the world out. Miguelito keeps inviting it in.

Under the hospitality he is still a working vehicle, and proud of it. A compound-turbo Duramax L5P does the pulling, chosen to purr: a house-trained kitten with thirteen hundred pound-feet in reserve, breathing through an Allison automatic and a full-float truck axle, riding on air that can lift him over a bad driveway or settle him into a parade crawl. The brakes are as big as the wheels allow. The tank holds 200 miles of range, because a good host never watches the gauge. Eight doors do the rest: the forward pairs swing like gentlemen, the rear pairs swing like villains, and the center pair opens together as a French-door gate, the front door of a house that happens to travel.

His signature run works west with the light: tacos at the downtown Mercado, ordered in Spanish and eaten standing up, then the long climb to Mulholland with the passengers up top and Griffith Observatory riding its ridge, down to Malibu for lobster at a picnic table, and the Santa Monica Pier for sunset. Passing traffic should be warned that overtaking Miguelito is a serial event: the nose, the door, the door, the door, and then, just when you believe in endings, the fin. He keeps two suits, tangerine over copper-bronze on hexagonal titanium for the road and formal Brewster greens on painted steel when the occasion wants a collar, because a host dresses for the room. For now he is a fantasy, a full spec and a standing invitation with no car to run it. If the right Stageway ever follows me home, this card graduates. Until then the tour departs whenever you like, at parade pace, with the roof open and Miguelito already sure you are hungry.

gallery.caption: Miguelito, the host. Big, silver, and already sure you are hungry.
The Mulholland tour at golden hour: passengers up top, the Observatory on its ridge, the basin below.
The neutral studio, in his road suit: tangerine over copper-bronze on hexagonal titanium, coffee canvas, cream within.
Company manners at the Theme Building, LAX, with the center gate open.
The one that got away: the Renton car as advertised, nose first. Not mine. The idea was.

title: Pixels
subtitle: Supercharged Hayabusa Power & Ligurian Coast Study
summary: An engine in search of a car found a cute one. A 1962 Fiat 600 in Italian-flag halftone dots, powered by a stroked and supercharged Hayabusa at about 300 WHP: feral as a wildcat, agile as a cat, and aimed at the curvy roads of the Ligurian coast.
thumb: Fantasies/62 Fiat 600 halftone flag colors on a fantasy Ligurian coast.jpg
heroImage: Fantasies/62 Fiat 600 halftone flag colors on a fantasy Ligurian coast.jpg
thumbnail: Fantasies/62 Fiat 600 halftone flag colors on a fantasy Ligurian coast.jpg

specifications.platform: 1962 Fiat 600 Custom, chopped 1 inch: the cute little car an unreasonable engine went looking for.
specifications.engine: Suzuki Hayabusa inline-four, stroked to 1,507cc and supercharged. The displacement is the catalog 3mm-over, 5mm-stroke stroker combination, rated past 240 hp before boost.
specifications.output: About 300 WHP, a conservative rung for the combination: bolt-on Rotrex supercharger kits for this engine are rated at 300 to 360 hp at the wheel.
specifications.transmission: A repackaged car transaxle in the pattern the Hayabusa aftermarket already sells: the 6-speed sequential, with a reverse gear and a limited-slip differential added for car duty.
specifications.performance: 1.35g lateral acceleration. The number is the commitment: if it takes flares and lowering to reach it when the design nears project stage, that is what the car gets.
specifications.character: Feral. Riding a wildcat: a cat's maneuverability, fun that runs active to violent, and no McLaren-style refinement anywhere in it.
specifications.finish: Halftone dot livery in the colors of the Italian flag. The dots are the pixels.
specifications.name: Pixels, named on 2026-10-20: a halftone image is built out of dots, and dots are pixels.
specifications.setting: A curvy road on the Ligurian coast, a town and what looks like an impressive old Roman bridge in the background: a romantic, fun Italian setting, chosen because the curves exist to really drive the car.
specifications.purpose: A road car built around one sentence: hey, that would be fun. Not a race car, and nobody is making grocery runs in it.
specifications.status: Fantasy: an engine-first design study, verified against the real Hayabusa car-conversion aftermarket. Fitment details stay open until the design gets close to becoming a project.

narrative: Pixels starts with an engine, the way the Fireball does. At a car show, my buddy got excited over a motorcycle engine in a Mini, and the engine was, I believe, a Hayabusa. I like weird engine combinations, so I went and investigated the Hayabusa, and the investigation sold it: serious output from the factory, and a real aftermarket behind it, clear down to cradles and repackaged car units built to put that engine into small cars. Which raised the obvious question. If not the Mini, what car? A Fiat turned up about then, and it seemed like a good fit.

Understand the numbers and the cute falls away. A stroked, supercharged Hayabusa making about 300 horsepower at the wheels, in a car that started life at about 1,300 pounds, is not a refined instrument. Pixels is feral. Present it as riding a wildcat: a cat brings impressive maneuverability to the fight, so the agility here is feline reflex rather than supercar polish, and the fun runs active to violent, nothing like the refined power of a McLaren. It stays a road car. It is not a race car, and nobody is making grocery runs in it a few days a week.

The specification is not hand-waving, either. The 1,507cc displacement is a catalog stroker combination for the Hayabusa, three millimeters over and five millimeters of stroke, rated past 240 horsepower before boost. Bolt-on Rotrex supercharger kits for the engine are rated at 300 to 360 horsepower at the wheel, so Pixels at about 300 is running a conservative tune, not a hopeful one. The transmission follows the repackaged car units the aftermarket already builds: the Hayabusa six-speed sequential, with a reverse gear and a limited-slip differential added for car duty. The 1.35g on the skidpad is the commitment the rest of the car answers to. If reaching it takes flares and lowering when the design gets close to a project, then flares and lowering are what it gets. The numbers rule. The hardware list can wait.

The paint came out of the same noodling season as the engine. I was looking at halftone schemes at the time, so the Fiat got the colors of the Italian flag built out of halftone dots, and a halftone dot is a pixel from the printing world: that is where the name lives. For the hero shot I asked for a romantic, fun setting in Italy and got a curvy road on the Ligurian coast, a town in the background, and what looks like an impressive old Roman bridge. The curves are the point. That road exists to really drive the car, and driving it is the whole fantasy: a cute little car, an unreasonable engine, and a wildcat underneath. Related design study: see Il Lungo: Stretched Fiat Paint Experiment, the same Italian proportions stretched long.

title: Crackerbox Series
subtitle: The Least Aerodynamic Truck of the Postwar Era, Given Enough Power
summary: Studies in a single question: what is the least aerodynamic truck of the postwar era, and what does it take to make the wall fast? Five GMC Crackerbox forward-control studies, ramp truck to 6x6, built around a Duramax and useful work.

specifications.platform: GMC F/D-series Crackerbox forward-control COE: all-aluminum tilt cab, 48-inch bumper-to-back-of-cab, built 1959-1968, the whole run inside the smog-exempt years
specifications.nickname: Crackerbox: the truckers' name for the upright cab, a saltine cracker box stood on end. Reserved for this GMC series; other makers' boxy COEs need not apply.
specifications.thesis: What is the least aerodynamic truck of the postwar era, and what does it take to make the wall fast?
specifications.engine: GM Duramax 6.6L turbodiesel, compound turbocharged: the house engine for forward-control trucks, because the V8 fits under the cab furthest
specifications.output: Sized to the scare: roughly 500 hp at the wheels pushes the wall to 100 mph; torque and gearing own the mud and the loaded pass
specifications.chassis: Almost a house recipe: cab swapped onto a spec donor chassis where one fits, otherwise a good set of parallel channel rails with a purpose-built performance suspension. The 6x6 keeps its M35A2 military frame, where everything already fits.
specifications.suspension: Air, with real anti-roll control: the wall's enemies are roll and crosswind wander
specifications.brakes: Air brakes, discs preferred; the donor choice sets the ceiling (detail parked for later research)
specifications.sound: Unrestricted by design: in a power application the engine may announce the wall. The cab gets the engineered passenger environment instead.
specifications.purpose: Private useful work, no towing and no OTR freight: car transport (flatbed or ramp), display transport in a permanent box, motorhome conversion, roll-off, recovery; road or off-road, two or three axles
specifications.status: Fantasy: a study set across the big-truck trade space. The 6x6's placement (this card, the Wilderness Recovery Vehicle grouping, or both) is still open.

narrative: Start with a rude question: what is the least aerodynamic truck of the postwar era? My answer is a GMC. In 1959 GMC built a Class 8 cabover so short and square that the whole cab, bumper to back glass, measured 48 inches, an aluminum box that tilted forward for service and existed for one reason: length laws. A shorter tractor meant a longer trailer, and driver comfort was not in the budget. The truckers who had to live in it named it the Crackerbox, for a saltine cracker box stood on end, and they did not mean it kindly. I have adopted the insult as a title of honor, and I reserve it for this GMC series alone. Other makers built boxy forward-control trucks. This one is boxier, with the most vertical windshield of the lot.

The studies on this card ask the follow-up: what does it take to make the wall fast? Scary, in my usage, is a place to visit, not a place to live, and the visits come in three kinds. Fast and empty on the open road, which is a horsepower bill from the air: roughly 500 hp at the wheels to see 100 mph in something shaped like this. Chewing through a mud bog with ease, which is torque, low gears, and traction, with horsepower as a spectator. And passing traffic fully loaded, which is midrange reserve, speed gained at highway pace with weight aboard. That last one has an audience. Somewhere ahead is a driver watching a metal wall fill his mirror, then his window, then his memory.

The pictures are studies, not builds: five cells in a trade space my big-truck fantasies share. Car transport on a flatbed or a ramp, display transport in a permanent box, motorhome conversion, roll-off work (currently assigned to a Mack FC in another study), and recovery, crossed with road or off-road and two axles or three. Towing is out; I do not envision it as a primary function for any build. Commercial freight boxes are out too. I am a private owner with a real rollback project already, and these are explorations toward what I like best. The orange 6x6 may yet emigrate to a Wilderness Recovery Vehicle grouping, or live in both places. The other four are staying right here, variations on one theme.

The recipe is nearly a house recipe by now. A Duramax does the pushing, chosen for a packaging reason: the V8 fits under a forward-control cab furthest, and under-cab volume is the scarcest thing these trucks have. Compound turbos, an Allison, and no apologies for the sound: in a power application the engine is allowed to announce the wall, and the cab gets engineered insulation instead of a quieter engine. The cab goes onto a donor chassis that meets spec where one exists, or onto a good set of parallel rails with a suspension built for the purpose. The 6x6 keeps its M35A2 military frame, because everything on it already fits and only the cab needs re-engineering. Air brakes and tire speed ratings are the honest limits, noted for later research. The wall was never the problem. The wall is the point.

specifications.shell: 1964 Ford Ranchero unibody, the second of two '64s; Floyd, the pink one running on its original inline six, is not this car
specifications.donor: 2011 Nissan Juke AWD, complete and running; bumper and front lights sheared off in a low-speed collision, everything else intact
specifications.engine: Nissan MR16DDT 1.6L direct-injection turbo four, 188 hp and 177 lb-ft, factory ECU and tune retained
specifications.layout: Transverse powertrain with power take-off unit, two-piece propshaft, and the Juke's torque-vectoring rear coupling: all-wheel drive in a 1964 unibody
specifications.transmission: OPEN PROBLEM: the factory CVT keeps the AWD but caps practical torque near 200 lb-ft; the RS6F94R 6-speed manual is proven at 300 whp but was only ever sold as front-wheel drive, so manual plus AWD is unproven
specifications.subframes: Juke front and rear subframes carried over as geometry jigs, on fabricated mounts with unibody reinforcement; rear subframe packaged under the bed with tank and exhaust
specifications.wheelbase: 109.5 in (Ranchero) vs 99.6 in (Juke): the 9.9 in gap is bridged by a two-piece propshaft whose carrier-bearing crossmember ties into structure, not floor pan
specifications.track: About 5 in wider than the Falcon platform, split among deepened inner tubs, wheel offset, and fabricated METAL flares
specifications.suspension: Juke MacPherson struts on fabricated turrets tied into the aprons and cowl; the Falcon's shock towers are removed
specifications.electronics: The Juke's whole nervous system comes across: harness, cluster, EPS column, immobilizer, CVT, AWD, and ABS modules, so the torque vectoring keeps the sensors it reasons from
specifications.intercooler: Front-mount, behind the Ranchero grille; a bolt-on the factory tune tolerates
specifications.power: OPEN INVESTIGATION: the 'just swap' baseline is the plan (the Ranchero is roughly 600 lb lighter than the Juke, so stock power already goes further); practical wringing beyond that is under research
specifications.name: Juke Joint: the donor is a Juke; the other half of the pun is the roadhouse
specifications.status: Fantasy by ruling (2026-11-03): meets the Dream definition, donor in hand and shell assigned, but stays a Fantasy until it gets more real. No work has begun.

narrative: Juke Joint started with somebody else's bad day. My wife's 2011 Nissan Juke caught a low-speed hit that sheared off its bumper and front lights, and left everything else intact: a complete, running, all-wheel-drive car with a turbocharged engine, suddenly worth more as an idea than as a Juke. I own two 1964 Rancheros. One is Floyd, pink and running on his original six, and he is not involved in this. The other one is a shell looking for a reason, and the name arrived before the plan did: the donor is a Juke, the venue is a joint, and the car is Juke Joint.

The build is a whole-car transplant, not an engine swap. Everything crosses over as a system: the MR16DDT turbo four, the transaxle, the power take-off, the torque-vectoring rear coupling, both subframes, the full wiring harness, the instrument cluster, the electric steering column, and every module that talks to them. Modern systems fail in cascades when you amputate pieces, so nothing gets amputated. The Juke subframes serve as geometry jigs on fabricated mounts, the Falcon's shock towers come out, and fabricated strut turrets tied into the aprons and cowl take their place. The Ranchero keeps its face and its bed. Underneath, it becomes a Juke that went to finishing school in 1964.

The two hard numbers are honest ones. The Ranchero's wheelbase is 109.5 inches and the Juke's is 99.6, so a two-piece propshaft with a carrier bearing bridges the 9.9 inches, its crossmember tied into structure rather than floor pan. The Juke's track is about five inches wider than the Falcon's, and the difference is split three ways: deepened inner tubs, wheel offset, and fabricated metal flares. Readers of the ScapeGoat card will note that car gets widened quarters and no flares, ever. Different car, different style. This one wears flares.

Two problems stay open on purpose, because solving them on paper would be lying. The transmission is a fork: keep the CVT and the all-wheel drive stays, but the CVT's practical ceiling is about 200 lb-ft of torque, a limit Nissan itself respected when it detuned the Nismo RS AWD. The 6-speed manual is proven at 300 wheel horsepower, but Nissan only ever sold it driving the front wheels, so manual plus all-wheel drive is unproven country. Power is the second: the stock swap already wins on arithmetic, since the Ranchero is roughly 600 pounds lighter than the Juke, and wringing out more is an investigation, not a promise. This card stays a Fantasy by my ruling. The build meets my own definition of a Dream, parts in hand and plan adjudicated, but the queue ahead of it is daunting and the parts deserve photographs before promotion. It promotes when it gets more real.

title: 1939 Ford COE Carnivore RV Restomod
subtitle: Supercharged 5.2L Long-Haul Overland Hauler
summary: A 1939 Ford Cab-Over-Engine RV restomod powered by a supercharged 5.2L Carnivore V8 (720 hp / 640 lb-ft) and 10R140 10-speed transmission, engineered specifically for high-speed desert blasts and steep mountain passes.

specifications.chassis: Custom Boxed Chassis w/ IFS & Coilovers

narrative: Forged from the bones of a 1939 Ford COE, the heart of this restomod is Ford's supercharged 5.2-liter Carnivore V8 delivering 640 lb-ft of torque and 720 horsepower managed by Ford's heavy-duty 10R140 TorqShift 10-speed automatic transmission, delivering lightning-fast gear changes and relentless acceleration without missing a beat under load.

Riding on a custom boxed chassis fitted with independent front suspension and adjustable coil-over shocks, the rig is built for effortless highway cruising and confident mountain ascents. It is spec'd directly for purpose-driven long-haul runs out of Los Angeles: effortlessly holding pace during high-speed desert blasts to Las Vegas, tackling the steep grade and sub-zero conditions on ski trips up to Mammoth, or carving through the sweepers along Highway 395 and the Pacific Coast Highway. Engineering precision meets raw, unstoppable capability.

title: The Talladega Transaxle: '69 Mid-Engine Concept
subtitle: The Cancelled '69 Supercar Study
summary: A radical, mid-engine concept fusing Ford's low-drag 1969 Torino Talladega aero nose with a mid-mounted 427 Cammer SOHC V8 and GT40 Hewland transaxle.
narrative: HISTORICAL DISCLAIMER: This vehicle concept, narrative, and historical background are entirely fictional. Project 69-M is an alternate-history design study exploring a what if crossover between Ford's NASCAR aero program and Le Mans mid-engine architecture.

This single prototype is all that remains of Project 69-M, Ford's radical, black-budget attempt to rewrite the rules of both NASCAR and the street. The concept was a direct fusion: take the low-drag, extended nose and flush grille of the homologation-bound 1969 Torino Talladega and mount it on a mid-engine chassis.

While the race cars would always be front-engine (NASCAR rules demanded it), Ford planned to sell 500 mid-engine T-Transaxles as a production vehicle, creating an exotic aero-king to beat Ferrari on the street and Dodge on the high banks. The large mid-body intakes, seen on the production C8 Corvette-like profile, were designed to feed a planned massive mid-ship powertrain.

To explain its mid-engine architecture, Ford engineers created the ultimate what if setup: They took a race-ready 7.0-liter (427 cu in) Ford Cammer SOHC V8, but instead of mounting it in the front, they reversed it, mounting it directly behind the driver. The original Ford Toploader transmission was scrapped. Instead, the Cammer was mated to a custom-cast, heavy-duty Hewland LG transaxle—the same reliable box used in Ford's GT40 program.

This '69 prototype, thus, was not just a styling exercise; it was an authentic integration of Ford's two greatest performance eras, pairing the high-drag oval-track nose with the mid-ship transaxle of Le Mans. The modern, 5-spoke alloys and updated side intakes were added decades later during a modern sympathetic restoration, preparing it for a single, high-speed test run on the gravel road of the skunkworks' private facility.

narrative: This one starts with a car I have not bought. A 1960 Jaguar Mark IX turned up in Redondo Beach, factory right-hand drive, black on black, factory sunroof, the complete original 3.8 and automatic still in it, standing at the curb with its headlamps out like a dowager who has mislaid her spectacles. It is a fantasy, and a fantasy can be built all the way.

The big Marks were saloons, and a saloon, properly understood, is a private room that moves. Jaguar sold Grace, Space, and Pace, and the stock car delivers the first two beautifully and the third in the manner of 1960, which is to say eventually. The fantasy keeps the room exactly as it is, picnic tables in the seatbacks and all, and attends to the pace.

Three affordable V12s presented themselves, and the choice was made on character as much as engineering. The Mercedes M120 is the most modern core, the BMW M73 the most dependable as bought, but the Jaguar's own V12 is the narrowest of the three, has the deepest aftermarket in the world, and suffers from failure modes that are all ancillary: heat, hoses, ignition, management, every one of them with a published cure. A long, narrow twelve in a long, narrow engine bay. The romantic pick and the defensible pick turned out to be the same engine.

So the V12 is stroked to 6.1 litres on its stock bore, forged pistons, flat-head architecture, and two small turbos exiled to the front wings where their heat cannot cook the bay, blowing 10 psi through a charge cooler hidden behind that tall grille. The result is about 675 hp and 740 lb-ft arriving as a plateau rather than a peak, because a saloon should waft first and strike second. A built 4L80E does the shifting, independent suspension minds both ends, new discs as big as the wheels will accept do the stopping, and the gearing is chosen so the car cruises at highway speed sitting on the torque peak in third, direct drive, ready to climb a grade or leave a light without consulting the overdrive. The wheels are forged three-piece twenties, centres tinted toward copper, the car lowered on air bags until the great hull settles into something sleeker, the rubber tucked into the wells like a secret kept politely.

The name took the longest of anything on this card. I have some sympathy for the men who named racing ships, because they had the same problem: a fast thing that must also behave in company. In 1938 a young Eric Newby signed aboard the four-masted barque Moshulu for the last of the grain races out of Australia, and wrote the best book ever made from inside that world, funny and unsentimental and exact about what a ship is. The tea clippers were gone by his time, but the standard he describes is theirs: speed was a cargo, dignity was the ballast. Ariel was a tea clipper of 1865, built by Robert Steele of Greenock, reckoned by her contemporaries the most beautiful of the fleet, and famous for a race in 1866 when she and Taeping came home from China 14,000 miles and docked twenty minutes apart after 99 days at sea. She was not the overlord of the clippers. She was the one inspired by dignity, and competently fast, first home in 1868. That is precisely the brief for this car. Her name carries a second cargo, buried where only the curious dig: Ariel is Hebrew for Lion of God, the archangel set over the earth and its creatures, centuries before Shakespeare borrowed the name for his airy spirit. A lion is a cat. This cat is a Jaguar. The clipper, the spirit, and the lion were travelling together all along.

Her livery came off a model of the ship and is a working vessel's uniform translated into deep lacquer. Black topsides above the waterline, copper sheathing below it, and a pale sheer stripe at the join: so the Jaguar wears warm brown-black above its swage line, a ruddy copper below it, evolved into an elegant automotive finish rather than raw hull metal, and a stripe between them in a very slight rose cream. Inside, the copper comes aboard as leather, the famous reddish tan the Italians simply call Cuoio, with cream piping in the stripe's own rose cream and the picnic-table wood warm alongside. The honest numbers for the whole arrangement: nought to sixty in the mid fours, the quarter in the high elevens at about 120, nine-tenths of a g on street rubber, and understeer when dignity finally runs out, because 4,550 pounds of saloon should bow before it misbehaves. A gentleman's rocket, crewed by a lion, named for the most beautiful ship in the tea trade.

specifications.brakes: New discs all around, as big as will fit
specifications.car: 1960 Jaguar Mark IX saloon, the Redondo Beach car: factory right-hand drive, factory sunroof, complete original 3.8 and automatic, clean title
specifications.engine: Jaguar V12 stroked to 6.1 litres on the stock 90 mm bore with an 80 mm crank, flat-head architecture, forged pistons at about 8.5:1, aftermarket rods, standalone engine management
specifications.gearing: Final drive follows the wheel and tyre choice, with a stated intent: highway speed should sit at the torque peak in 3rd gear, direct, not overdrive, for a good leave, hill climbing, and respectable times on the open road. On the chosen 28.7 in tyre, a final drive in the 3.55 to 3.73 window puts 75 mph between about 3,100 and 3,300 rpm in 3rd, inside the plateau
specifications.induction: Twin small turbos mounted in the front wings at 10 psi, chosen to exile turbo heat from the engine bay; charge cooler packaged behind the Mark IX's tall grille
specifications.interior: The saloon as a private room: ceremony, enclosure, and picnic tables in the seatbacks. The leather is the famous copper-red luxury hide tone, Ferrari's Cuoio and Hermès' fauve family: a rich reddish-copper tan matched to the ruddy lower body, carried across seats and door cards and set off with cream piping in the same slight rose cream as the body's dividing stripe. Black retreats to the dash top and headliner, and the seatback wood stays in the same warm family (Scot's calls, 2026-11-07)
specifications.livery: Clipper two-tone from the tea clipper Ariel, in deep lacquer: warm brown-black gloss above the swage line (roof, pillars, bonnet, upper doors and wings) over ruddy copper below it (lower doors, sills, lower wings and quarters), the copper a morphed, elegant automotive finish rather than raw hull metal, separated by a thin stripe in a very slight rose cream
specifications.name: Ariel, the tea clipper of 1865: not the overlord of the fleet, but the one inspired by dignity and competently fast, first home in the 1868 tea season after her photo-finish race of 1866
specifications.performance: Estimated 0 to 60 in 4.4 to 4.8 seconds; quarter mile 11.6 to 12.1 at 117 to 121 mph on street tyres, about 11.2 to 11.5 on drag radials; skidpad 0.85 to 0.90 g on 300-treadwear street rubber, 0.95 to 1.00 g on track rubber; limit behaviour is dignified understeer
specifications.power: An estimated 675 hp and 740 lb-ft, with the torque plateau running from about 2,400 to 4,800 rpm (assistant's estimates, not promises)
specifications.rearSuspension: Independent rear suspension on a hardened cradle; the centre section (hardened Ford 8.8 or an aftermarket 9-inch IRS) is an engineering detail for build time, since both stand up to the load at this boost
specifications.status: Fantasy, complete as a card. The car itself is not bought.
specifications.transmission: Built GM 4L80E automatic, the gearbox Jaguar itself paired with the 6.0 V12, with lockup converter and 0.75 overdrive
specifications.wheels: Forged three-piece wheels in the Forgeline pattern, the consensus choice on big-car restomod builds: 20 x 8.5 in front and 20 x 10 in rear, medium-profile rubber (245/45 front, 275/40 rear, overall diameter about 28.7 in, close to stock) tucked into the wells, the car lowered on air bags to a sleeker ride height. Centers are tinted toward the ruddy copper of the lower body (Scot's call, 2026-11-07), polished lips
specifications.suspension: SLA front and IRS rear (see frontSuspension and rearSuspension), ride height on air bags, lowered from stock for a sleeker line
